newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish forester SCA's profits dive.
newsitem.headline: Swedish forester SCA's profits dive.

text.p: Svenska Cellulosa Aktiebolaget, Sweden's largest forestry company, Thursday said profits fell 38 percent last year, hurt by lower prices and slack demand affecting the Swedish pulp and paper industry.
SCA reported a profit after financial items of 3.57 billion crowns ($492 million) compared with 5.73 billion crowns ($790 million) in 1995.
Echoing the gloomy tone of rival Stora, which also reported sharply lower profits, SCA said the pricing outlook remained uncertain for 1997.
"The recovery is taking place from a low level at a slow pace. Major uncertainty remains for price developments surrounding pulp and recycling paper," SCA said.

Analysts said Sweden's forest products industry, one of the world's largest, needed to focus on cutting costs as the prospect of price rises remained distant and profits were likely to remain under pressure in 1997.
"1997 will still be a weak year, much like 1996. But this year will be stronger in the second half and 1998 should be better," one Stockholm-based analyst said.
Sales fell to 55.41 billion crowns ($7.64 billion) from 65.32 billion ($9 billion).
The drop in profits was about in line with analysts' forecasts. SCA shares were unchanged at 144 crowns ($19.85) in late trading.
In the Swedish forestry sector, MoDo is due to report its 1996 results on Feb. 19 and AssiDoman AB on Feb. 20.
Analysts said SCA was somewhat better off than other companies because its hygiene products division cushioned it from the drop in pulp prices.
Profit for hygiene products, the company's largest unit, which includes clinical products as well as tissue, rose 70 percent last year, larger than expected, analysts said.
Stora, Sweden's No. 2 forest products company, on Wednesday said its profits tumbled 71 percent to 2.35 billion crowns ($323.9 million).

"The companies that will do best are those that are getting to grip with the cost structure and getting costs under control. I think SCA is doing this," said Denis Christie, forestry analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
